extracted.intended_audience: health journalists, press-release writers, health PR professionals, and researchers seeking media coverage
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist-style evaluation of health/medical press releases (the HealthNewsReview 10 criteria plus cross-cutting items) used to judge whether a release provides the information journalists need and is 'pickup-worthy' by quality outlets. Applies to releases about treatments, tests, products, and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release state the cost of the treatment/test/product (acquisition price, insurance coverage, out-of-pocket)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schwitzer found cost is the most-omitted item in news. Release writers should state explicit cost information where relevant (list price, typical insurance coverage, likely out-of-pocket costs) rather than leaving reporters to guess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release give absolute benefit (e.g., '5 fewer deaths per 1,000 patients') rather than relative-risk language ('a 50% reduction')?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer absolute numbers and natural frequencies to relative risks; include baseline risk so readers can judge clinical significance. Avoid presenting only relative reductions, which can exaggerate perceived benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Are adverse events, side effects, and dropouts reported with the same prominence as benefits?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report harms using the same metrics and prominence as benefits (absolute numbers/percentages, rates). Don't bury harms in fine print or omit common/serious adverse events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release identify study type (RCT, observational, in vitro, animal model), sample size, and key methodological limits?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the study design, sample size, main limitations, and whether results are preliminary. Distinguish between preclinical (animal/in vitro), observational, and randomized controlled evidence so readers can assess strength of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease-mongering check
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release exaggerate the prevalence or severity of the underlying condition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid widening disease definitions or overstating how common/serious a condition is to make results seem more important. Pickup-worthy releases avoid 'disease-mongering' used to bait coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Are independent experts (not co-authors, not paid by sponsor) named and quoted, with their contact details?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide named, independent experts (with contact details) who can comment; do not rely solely on study authors or sponsor-paid spokespeople. Independent commentary increases credibility and allows reporters to seek outside perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with existing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release compare the new treatment/test to existing options, including doing nothing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the new intervention in context by comparing effectiveness, risks, costs, and accessibility with current standards of care or non-intervention. Avoid presenting the new option as if no alternatives exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the treatment available now? FDA-approved? Investigational? Available only at the trial site?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about current availability and regulatory status (approved, investigational, limited access). Clarify whether findings apply to a widely available product or to a limited research setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty claim accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the release claims novelty, is the claim accurate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schwitzer flags inflated 'first ever' claims as a major source of error. Verify and qualify novelty claims (e.g., 'first randomized trial in X population' vs. 'first ever') and avoid hyperbolic phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press-release-only sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the news story rely only on the press release?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schwitzer treats press-release-only sourcing as a quality failure for journalism — for release writers, this implies releases should themselves contain enough independent material (data, methods, independent quotes, context) that a story based only on the release would still be substantively complete. Do not assume reporters will or should supplement the release with outside research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict-of-interest disclosure (bonus, cross-cutting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are funder, ownership, and personal financial ties of investigators disclosed at the front of the release rather than buried at the bottom?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose funding sources, sponsor involvement, and investigators' relevant financial ties prominently (ideally early in the release). Burying COI statements undermines transparency and can mislead readers and journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness implication
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases that pre-satisfy the 10 criteria are substantially more likely to be used verbatim by quality outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schwitzer's data show that quality outlets (e.g., NYT, NPR, AP) prefer releases that meet these criteria; such releases earn HealthNewsReview's highest ratings and are more likely to be reproduced as-is. Conversely, releases failing on costs, quality-of-evidence, and independent sources score very low even when factually accurate — so meeting these criteria increases chances of high-quality pickup.
